nodes.label: Hammurabi and the Amorite Kingdoms
nodes.full: The Old Babylonian world the Kassites inherit — Marduk's rising cult, the abandoned south and the Sealand, the Hittite raid that empties the throne. See babylon-2004bc-1595bc.
nodes.src: background — see the folio babylon-2004bc-1595bc.

nodes.label: The Second Dynasty of Isin
nodes.full: The native Babylonian dynasty that rises after the Elamite sack — Nebuchadnezzar I recovers the statue of Marduk and makes him supreme. See babylon-1155bc-539bc.
nodes.src: background — see the folio babylon-1155bc-539bc.

nodes.label: The Middle Assyrian Kingdom
nodes.full: The rival northern kingdom — Ashur-uballit who makes a king of Babylon, Adad-nirari and Shalmaneser who take the Jazira, Tukulti-Ninurta who conquers Babylon itself. See assyria-1400bc-1050bc.
nodes.src: background — see the folio assyria-1400bc-1050bc.

nodes.label: Elam
nodes.full: The southwest-Iranian power — a target of Kurigalzu I, then the invader that under Shutruk-Nahhunte sacks Babylon in 1158, ends the dynasty, and carries the great Mesopotamian monuments to Susa.
nodes.src: background — Daniel Potts, 'The Archaeology of Elam' (1999).

nodes.label: The Amarna world
nodes.full: The Late Bronze system of Great Kingdoms — Egypt, Hatti, Mitanni — with which Kassite Babylonia corresponds, trades and intermarries as an equal. See egypt-1550bc-1200bc.
nodes.src: background — see the folio egypt-1550bc-1200bc; Moran, 'The Amarna Letters' (1992).

nodes.label: A Zagros people become the kings of Babylon
nodes.full: The Kassites — a people from the Zagros speaking a language related to nothing else known — had lived in Babylonia as soldiers and farm labour since the late Old Babylonian period. When the Hittite raid left the throne empty they took it, and held it for thirty-six kings across more than four centuries, the longest dynasty in Mesopotamian history. Within a generation they wrote, worshipped and ruled as Babylonians, keeping only their clan names and two dynastic gods.
nodes.src: J. A. Brinkman, 'Materials and Studies for Kassite History' I (1976); Bartelmus & Sternitzke (eds.), 'Karduniaš: Babylonia under the Kassites' (2017).

nodes.label: Agum II brings Marduk home
nodes.full: An inscription copied a thousand years later credits King Agum II with recovering the statues of Marduk and his consort from the land of Hana, twenty-four years after the Hittites carried them off, and re-installing them in the Esagila with fresh gold and lapis regalia. Whether or not the detail is accurate, restoring the god who had been stolen was the act by which the new mountain dynasty made itself Babylon's legitimate ruler.
nodes.src: The Agum-kakrime inscription (a Neo-Assyrian library copy); Benjamin Foster, 'Before the Muses' (2005), pp. 360–364.

nodes.label: Ulamburiash reunites Babylonia
nodes.full: For nearly three centuries after Samsu-iluna lost the south, a 'Sealand' dynasty had held the marshes and the old Sumerian cities. Around 1460 the Kassite king Ulamburiash conquered it, and for the first time since 1740 the whole of Babylonia — north and south — was under a single crown. The country now begins to be called by a single name in the diplomatic record: Karduniash.
nodes.src: Odette Boivin, 'The First Dynasty of the Sealand in Mesopotamia' (2018); Brinkman (1976).

nodes.label: Kurigalzu I, the builder-king
nodes.full: Kurigalzu I built a new royal capital near modern Baghdad, Dur-Kurigalzu, whose ziggurat still stands fifty-seven metres high, and restored the great temples of Ur, Uruk, Eridu and Nippur on a lavish scale. He campaigned against Elam and, by one account, took Susa. His reign is the high-water mark of Kassite wealth and prestige.
nodes.src: Taha Baqir's excavations at Aqar Quf (1942–45); Kurigalzu's building inscriptions in Brinkman (1976).

nodes.label: Burna-Buriash II and the brotherhood of kings
nodes.full: Burna-Buriash II and his predecessor wrote to Amenhotep III and Akhenaten of Egypt as fellow 'Great Kings' and 'brothers' — sending Babylonian lapis, horses and chariots for Egyptian gold, arranging royal marriages, and haggling over protocol and over a caravan robbed in Canaan. When Egypt received Assyrian envoys, Burna-Buriash protested: the Assyrians, he wrote, were his vassals, and had no business corresponding as equals.
nodes.src: William Moran, 'The Amarna Letters' (1992), EA 6–14; Brinkman (1976).

nodes.label: Assyria makes a king of Babylon
nodes.full: A Kassite king part-descended from the Assyrian royal house through a marriage alliance was murdered in a palace coup. Ashur-uballit I of Assyria marched south, killed the usurper, and set Kurigalzu II on the throne. It was the first time Assyria decided who ruled Babylon — the opening move of a rivalry between the two Mesopotamian kingdoms that would run for seven hundred years.
nodes.src: The 'Synchronistic History' and 'Chronicle P'; Brinkman, 'Materials and Studies for Kassite History' I (1976).

nodes.label: Kurigalzu II and Nazi-Maruttash hold the line
nodes.full: Kurigalzu II and his son Nazi-Maruttash fought the rising Assyrian kings Enlil-nirari and Adad-nirari I along the middle-Tigris border — Sugagu, Kilizi — to inconclusive results, and campaigned against Elam. It was a long standoff in which Assyria slowly gained ground. Nazi-Maruttash's reign is the likeliest setting for the poem Ludlul bel nemeqi.
nodes.src: The 'Synchronistic History'; Brinkman (1976); the border wars in A. K. Grayson, 'Assyrian Rulers of the Third and Second Millennia BC' (RIMA 1, 1987).

nodes.label: Kashtiliash IV, captured by Tukulti-Ninurta
nodes.full: Tukulti-Ninurta I of Assyria defeated Kashtiliash IV, seized him and led him bound to Assur; the Assyrians sacked Babylon, tore down its wall, plundered the Esagila and carried off the statue of Marduk. Tukulti-Ninurta then ruled Babylonia for about seven years, directly and through governors, taking the title 'king of Karduniash'. His court epic frames the whole campaign as Marduk's punishment of an oath-breaking king.
nodes.src: The 'Tukulti-Ninurta Epic' (Peter Machinist, 1978); 'Chronicle P'; RIMA 1 (Grayson 1987).

nodes.label: Adad-shuma-usur restores the dynasty
nodes.full: A Babylonian reaction ejected the Assyrian garrisons and put the Kassite line back on the throne under Adad-shuma-usur, who reigned some thirty years, raided into Assyria itself, and — by one chronicle's account — took a hand in deposing an Assyrian king in a time of Assyrian civil strife. It was the dynasty's last strong reign.
nodes.src: 'Chronicle P' and the 'Synchronistic History'; Brinkman, 'A Political History of Post-Kassite Babylonia' (1968), intro.

nodes.label: The Elamite sack and the end of the dynasty
nodes.full: Shutruk-Nahhunte of Elam and his son Kutir-Nahhunte invaded, sacked Babylon, Sippar and Eshnunna, and carried a hoard of plunder home to Susa — a hoard that included the statue of Marduk, the law stele of Hammurabi, the Victory Stele of Naram-Sin and the Manishtushu Obelisk, where French excavators found them in 1901. The last Kassite king, Enlil-nadin-ahi, was deposed and taken to Elam. The dynasty had lasted four hundred and forty years.
nodes.src: The Elamite inscriptions added to the looted monuments; Daniel Potts, 'The Archaeology of Elam' (1999), ch. 7.

nodes.label: Ethnic difference at the top, continuity below
nodes.full: The Kassites ruled as thoroughly Babylonian kings — Babylonian names, gods and titles — but kept a distinct ruling class organised into 'Houses' (bītu) named for clan ancestors, from which the governors and army commanders were drawn, and honoured two dynastic gods of their own, Shuqamuna and Shumaliya. Below that thin ethnic layer, Babylonian life, language and religion carried on unbroken.
nodes.src: Walter Sommerfeld, 'The Kassites of Ancient Mesopotamia' (in CANE, 1995); the 'House' system in Brinkman (1976).

nodes.label: The reconquest of the south
nodes.full: The First Sealand Dynasty had held the marsh south and the old Sumerian cities as an independent kingdom since Samsu-iluna lost them around 1740. The Kassite king Ulamburiash conquered it, reincorporating the alluvial heartland into Babylonia after nearly three centuries apart and ending the long north–south split within the country.
nodes.src: Odette Boivin, 'The First Dynasty of the Sealand in Mesopotamia' (2018).

nodes.label: The long border war with Assyria
nodes.full: From Ashur-uballit's intervention onward, Assyria and Babylonia fought a recurring war over the middle-Tigris border and the towns around Arrapha. Kurigalzu II clashed with Adad-nirari I at Sugagu; Nazi-Maruttash with the same king at Kar-Ishtar. No campaign was decisive, but across a century the frontier moved steadily in Assyria's favour, setting up the conquest that followed.
nodes.src: The 'Synchronistic History'; A. K. Grayson, 'Assyrian Rulers of the Third and Second Millennia BC' (RIMA 1, 1987).

nodes.label: Tukulti-Ninurta takes Babylon
nodes.full: Tukulti-Ninurta I broke Kashtiliash IV's army, captured the king, and led him in chains to Assur. His troops stormed Babylon, demolished its wall, looted the Esagila and carried Marduk's statue north. For about seven years an Assyrian king ruled Babylonia. His court poem, the 'Tukulti-Ninurta Epic', justifies the sack as the gods' verdict on a Kassite king who had broken a sworn treaty.
nodes.src: Peter Machinist, 'The Epic of Tukulti-Ninurta I' (1978); 'Chronicle P'.

nodes.label: The wars with Elam
nodes.full: Elam and Babylonia contested the eastern frontier and the Diyala throughout the period. Kurigalzu I raided deep into Elam and is said to have taken Susa; from the mid-twelfth century the Elamite kings Shutruk-Nahhunte and Kutir-Nahhunte raided Babylonia repeatedly, exploiting its weakness after the Assyrian occupation and preparing the ground for the final invasion.
nodes.src: Daniel Potts, 'The Archaeology of Elam' (1999), ch. 6–7; Brinkman (1976).

nodes.label: The invasion of 1158 and the loss of the monuments
nodes.full: The Elamite army swept through northern Babylonia, sacking Babylon, Sippar and Eshnunna in turn, and stripped their temples and squares of everything portable and ancient. The plunder taken back to Susa is why the great monuments of Mesopotamian history — Hammurabi's laws, Naram-Sin's victory, the Manishtushu land purchases, the statue of Marduk — were dug up in Iran rather than in Iraq.
nodes.src: The Elamite dedicatory inscriptions cut into the looted stones; Potts, 'The Archaeology of Elam' (1999).

nodes.label: The kudurru — the boundary stone
nodes.full: The kudurru is an inscribed stone monument recording a royal grant of land — its boundaries, its tax status, the witnesses, the date, and long curses on anyone who moves it — topped or ringed with carved emblems of a dozen or more gods called as guarantors. The stone was kept in a temple and a clay copy on the estate. About a hundred and sixty survive, and they are the single richest source for Kassite society.
nodes.src: Susanne Paulus, 'Die babylonischen Kudurru-Inschriften' (2014); Kathryn Slanski, 'The Babylonian Entitlement narûs (kudurrus)' (2003).

nodes.label: Land for service — the feudal turn
nodes.full: The kudurru grants alienated crown land in perpetuity to a rising class of officials and soldiers, very often with exemption from tax, from corvée, and from the billeting of troops. In return the grantees owed the king their loyalty and their service — above all the expensive chariotry. A large part of Babylonia's land, revenue and army thus passed into the hands of a privileged gentry, a partial feudalisation with no real precedent.
nodes.src: J. A. Brinkman, 'Materials and Studies for Kassite History' I (1976); the privileges (zakûtu) analysed in Paulus (2014).

nodes.label: The province and the governor's archive
nodes.full: Kassite Babylonia was divided into provinces under governors, each with a canal inspector and a chain of royal storehouses. A mid-Kassite archive of thousands of tablets from Nippur documents one province in close-up: the rations issued, the fields sown, the herds counted, the corvée mustered, the royal couriers fed. It is the most detailed picture of Babylonian provincial government between Ur III and the first millennium.
nodes.src: The Kassite Nippur archive; J. A. Brinkman, 'The Administration of Kassite Babylonia' and 'Materials and Studies' I (1976).

nodes.label: The rules of the Great Kings' club
nodes.full: Only a handful of rulers — Egypt, Hatti, Mitanni, Assyria, Babylonia, later Elam and Cyprus — were 'Great Kings' who addressed one another as 'brother'. The club had an etiquette: a fixed greeting formula, gifts of matched value, the loan of physicians and craftsmen, the safe-conduct of envoys, the terms of a marriage, and a recognised sharp register for when the rules were broken. It is the earliest developed system of interstate protocol.
nodes.src: Mario Liverani, 'Prestige and Interest: International Relations in the Near East ca. 1600–1100 BC' (1990); Cohen & Westbrook (eds.), 'Amarna Diplomacy' (2000).

nodes.label: Royal patronage and the fixed edition
nodes.full: The Kassite court paid for scholars to gather, edit and put in fixed order the great bodies of cuneiform learning — the omen compendia, the medical and incantation handbooks, the lexical lists, the hymns — producing standard 'serialised' editions organised by tablet and line. The master scholar, the ummânu, became a recognised court office. It is the bureaucratic act behind what scholars call the canonisation of Mesopotamian knowledge.
nodes.src: A. Leo Oppenheim, 'Ancient Mesopotamia' (1964), on the 'stream of tradition'; Francesca Rochberg, 'The Heavenly Writing' (2004).

nodes.label: Nippur revived and the prebend takes shape
nodes.full: The Kassites rebuilt the temples of Nippur and made Enlil's city a working administrative and religious centre again. And in the temple economy of this period the prebend hardens into an institution: a defined share of a temple's income and offerings, attached to a named priestly duty, which could be owned, split, leased, inherited and sold — property in a slice of the sacred.
nodes.src: Brinkman (1976); the Kassite prebend in the studies of Marten Stol and Muhammad Dandamayev's later comparanda.

nodes.label: The god who was carried off three times
nodes.full: Across this period Marduk climbed toward the head of the pantheon — but was not yet supreme, and his statue was taken from Babylon three times: to Hana by the Hittites, to Assur by Tukulti-Ninurta, to Susa by the Elamites. Each loss and each recovery (or hoped-for recovery) fed a theology of the god's 'journeys', his anger, his absence, and the chaos that fills a city its god has left.
nodes.src: W. G. Lambert, 'Babylonian Creation Myths' (2013); the 'Marduk Prophecy' and the statue's movements in Brinkman (1976).

nodes.label: The Kassite dynastic gods
nodes.full: Shuqamuna and Shumaliya, the Kassite royal couple, kept a shrine in Babylon and were invoked at the coronation of a Kassite king. Beyond that the dynasty took over the Babylonian gods entirely — its kings' names honour Marduk, Enlil, Nergal, Adad — and added nothing to the pantheon. It is religious assimilation that leaves the newcomers' identity as a thin, ceremonial layer over an unchanged Babylonian faith.
nodes.src: Walter Sommerfeld, 'The Kassites of Ancient Mesopotamia' (CANE, 1995); the dynastic gods in Brinkman (1976).

nodes.label: Enlil's city restored
nodes.full: The Kassite kings made a deliberate project of rehabilitating Nippur — rebuilding the Ekur, reviving its cult and its schools, and being seen to honour Enlil, still the god understood to grant legitimate rule over the whole land. A dynasty of foreign origin needed the oldest sanction it could get, and Nippur was where that sanction was conferred.
nodes.src: The Kassite building inscriptions from Nippur (Brinkman 1976); McGuire Gibson's Nippur excavation reports.

nodes.label: The god-lists and omen series fixed
nodes.full: Under royal patronage the reference works of Babylonian religion were given their standard form: the great god-list An = Anum, some two thousand divine names in a set order with their family relationships; the celestial-omen series Enuma Anu Enlil; the terrestrial-omen series Shumma alu; the extispicy and incantation series. These editions were then copied, tablet for tablet, into the libraries of the first millennium.
nodes.src: Wilfred Lambert on An = Anum; Francesca Rochberg, 'The Heavenly Writing' (2004); Nils Heeßel on the omen series.

nodes.label: Ludlul bel nemeqi — the Babylonian Job
nodes.full: A long poem, probably of Nazi-Maruttash's reign, in the voice of a high official — Shubshi-meshre-Shakkan — who loses his health, his wealth, his friends and his office though he can name no sin, endures the silence of the gods and the helplessness of the diviners, is given up for dead, and is then restored by Marduk through a sequence of dreams. It is the fullest ancient meditation on undeserved suffering before the Book of Job, which it foreshadows closely.
nodes.src: W. G. Lambert, 'Babylonian Wisdom Literature' (1960); Amar Annus & Alan Lenzi, 'Ludlul bēl nēmeqi: The Standard Babylonian Poem of the Righteous Sufferer' (2010).

nodes.label: The personal god, the demon and the two healers
nodes.full: Lived religion ran on the personal god and goddess, the crowd of demons (Lamashtu the child-snatcher, the lurking utukku), and the restless ghost. Two professions worked the sickbed together: the āšipu, the exorcist, who diagnosed and expelled a divine or demonic cause with ritual and incantation, and the asû, the physician, who treated with drugs, poultices and bandages. Their handbooks, too, were now being standardised.
nodes.src: JoAnn Scurlock, 'Sourcebook for Ancient Mesopotamian Medicine' (2014); Markham Geller, 'Ancient Babylonian Medicine' (2010).

nodes.label: The glazed moulded-brick facade
nodes.full: King Kara-indash built at Uruk a small temple for the goddess Inanna whose outer walls were made of specially moulded bricks that, assembled, formed a relief of alternating mountain and water deities holding overflowing vases. It is a technical breakthrough — a picture built into the structural brickwork — and the direct ancestor of the great glazed-brick facades of Nebuchadnezzar's Babylon a thousand years later.
nodes.src: The facade in the Vorderasiatisches Museum, Berlin; Ernst Heinrich, 'Die Tempel und Heiligtümer im alten Mesopotamien' (1982).

nodes.label: The carved kudurru
nodes.full: The boundary stones are also monuments of relief carving: the emblems of the gods — Marduk's spade, Nabu's stylus, the crescent, the sun-disc, the lightning-fork, the scorpion, the snake, the goddess's dog — arranged in tiers or wound around the stone as a visual roll-call of the divine witnesses, sometimes with a figured scene of the king handing land to the grantee. The style is elongated, dense, and heavy with symbol.
nodes.src: Ursula Seidl, 'Die babylonischen Kudurru-Reliefs' (1989).

nodes.label: The prized Kassite seal
nodes.full: Kassite seal-cutting produced two admired styles: an early one in which a standing worshipper shares the surface with a long, formal prayer to a god; and a later, exquisite manner of finely cut animals, sacred trees and cross-patterns in hard chalcedony. Kassite seals were valued far beyond Babylonia — a cache of them turned up in a Bronze Age palace at Thebes in Greece, carried there as treasure.
nodes.src: Dominique Collon, 'First Impressions: Cylinder Seals in the Ancient Near East' (1987); Edith Porada, 'The Cylinder Seals Found at Thebes in Boeotia' (1981).

nodes.label: The Standard Babylonian Gilgamesh
nodes.full: In this editing age the Gilgamesh epic received the twelve-tablet 'standard' version that would be copied across the Near East for a thousand years — the wall-of-Uruk prologue, Enkidu, the cedar forest, the death of the friend, the flood told by its survivor, and the failed quest for eternal life. Tradition credits the edition to a scholar named Sin-leqi-unninni, whose name later scribal families claimed as their founding ancestor.
nodes.src: Andrew George, 'The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic' (2003), vol. 1, on the Standard Babylonian version and Sin-leqi-unninni.

nodes.label: The Babylonian scale sung — the Hurrian hymns
nodes.full: From Ugarit on the Syrian coast, within the same cultural world, come the 'Hurrian hymns': cult songs written in Hurrian with the melody notated underneath in the very terms — string-names and interval-pairs — of the Old Babylonian tuning texts. The best preserved, the Hymn to Nikkal, is the oldest substantially complete notated tune known, and proof that the Babylonian theory of music was a living practice across the region.
nodes.src: Anne Draffkorn Kilmer, 'The Cult Song with Music from Ancient Ugarit' (RA 1974); Theo Krispijn and Raoul Vitale on the reconstruction.

nodes.label: The scholars as editors of the tradition
nodes.full: The Kassite intellectual achievement was curatorial. Scholars gathered scattered older manuscripts, chose between variant readings, split each work into numbered tablets linked by catch-lines, and issued authoritative editions of the omens, the medical and incantation handbooks, the lexical lists, the hymns and the epics. Scribes then copied those editions with little change for a thousand years. The 'canon' of cuneiform learning is essentially the library the Kassite scholars assembled.
nodes.src: A. Leo Oppenheim, 'Ancient Mesopotamia' (1964); Alan Lenzi, 'Secrecy and the Gods' (2008).

nodes.label: The named scholar and the scribal lineage
nodes.full: For the first time individual scholars are named as the authors or editors of works — Sin-leqi-unninni for Gilgamesh, and others for the omen and medical series — and scholarly families begin to trace their descent from such an 'ancestor', whose name becomes a professional surname carried for a millennium. Learning is now a heritable identity with a genealogy, guarded and transmitted within a caste.
nodes.src: Paul-Alain Beaulieu, 'The Descendants of Sin-leqi-unninni' (2000); Alan Lenzi, 'Secrecy and the Gods' (2008).

nodes.label: The star lists and the paths of the sky
nodes.full: Dated observation of the heavens went on, and scholars compiled lists of the fixed stars, the risings and settings through the year, and the paths of the moon and the planets against the star background. This is the raw material out of which, a few centuries later, the standard astronomical compendium MUL.APIN would be assembled — the systematic sky-map on which Babylonian astronomy was built.
nodes.src: Hermann Hunger & David Pingree, 'MUL.APIN: An Astronomical Compendium in Cuneiform' (1989); Francesca Rochberg, 'The Heavenly Writing' (2004).

nodes.label: Kassite as an object of study
nodes.full: Babylonian scribes drew up Kassite–Akkadian glossaries — the names of gods, of officials, of colours, of plants, and above all of horse-colours and horse-parts — and it is almost entirely from these lists that anything is known of the Kassite language today. That the ruling dynasty's own tongue survived only as a set of scholarly word-lists is a fair emblem of the age's cast of mind.
nodes.src: Kemal Balkan, 'Kassitenstudien 1: Die Sprache der Kassiten' (1954); recent work by Yigal Bloch and by the 'Karduniaš' volume (2017).

nodes.label: Reasoning about divine justice
nodes.full: Beneath its poetry, Ludlul bel nemeqi advances a position: that the will of the gods is genuinely unknowable, that what pleases a god today may offend him tomorrow, that even the professional diviner can be wrong, and yet that Marduk's mercy is real and comes to the sufferer who endures. The later 'Babylonian Theodicy' and the sardonic 'Dialogue of Pessimism' argue with this stance — a live philosophical debate about whether the universe is just.
nodes.src: W. G. Lambert, 'Babylonian Wisdom Literature' (1960); Karel van der Toorn, 'Sin and Sanction in Israel and Mesopotamia' (1985).

nodes.label: The recovery of the reunified south
nodes.full: Under the long Kassite peace and the reunification of the country, the south filled in again after the Old Babylonian collapse — survey shows the number and size of settlements rebounding sharply. But the new farmland followed new canal lines: the old Nippur–Isin axis stayed dead, and settlement clustered instead along the Tigris and to the east. The alluvial heartland was re-farmed, on a different map.
nodes.src: Robert McC. Adams, 'Heartland of Cities' (1981); J. A. Armstrong and Hermann Gasche on Kassite-period settlement.

nodes.label: Horse-breeding and the horse trade
nodes.full: Kassite Babylonia was known for its horses. The kings bred them on royal studs, the Nippur archives and the boundary stones track them by name and colour, and 'Kassite horses' and chariots were a standard entry in the gift-lists of the Amarna letters and a prized import at Nuzi and in Egypt. Horse-raising was a specialist, high-value industry tied to the chariot elite.
nodes.src: J. A. Brinkman, 'Materials and Studies for Kassite History' I (1976); horse terms in the Kassite glossaries (Balkan 1954); the Amarna gift-lists.

nodes.label: Glass and glazed ware
nodes.full: Glassmaking moved from occasional beads to an organised luxury craft: core-formed vessels, coloured canes, mosaic glass and inlays for furniture and jewellery, alongside glazed pottery and the glazed moulded brick. The recipes — quartz sand or crushed pebbles fused with plant-ash soda and lime, coloured with copper, cobalt and lead — were trade secrets, and the finished goods were exported.
nodes.src: A. Leo Oppenheim et al., 'Glass and Glassmaking in Ancient Mesopotamia' (1970); Peter Moorey, 'Ancient Mesopotamian Materials and Industries' (1994).

nodes.label: The prebend and the temple as an institution
nodes.full: The temple was landlord, employer and bank, staffed by dedicated oblates and run on defined shares of its income — prebends — that individuals owned, split, leased and passed to their heirs. Endowed with land, exempt from much taxation, and rooted in the oldest institutions of the country, the temple estates were the sector that best rode out the political shocks of the period.
nodes.src: Marten Stol on the Babylonian prebend; Brinkman (1976); comparanda in Muhammad Dandamayev's temple-economy studies.

nodes.label: Bulk luxury trade under the Great-King peace
nodes.full: The century of relative peace among the Great Kingdoms let the long-distance luxury trade flourish. Babylonian caravans carried lapis lazuli, horses and manufactures to Egypt for gold; goods moved by ship around the eastern Mediterranean, as the cargo of the Uluburun wreck — lapis, tin, ebony, ivory, faience — shows. Babylonia was a node in a genuinely interconnected Bronze Age economy.
nodes.src: Cemal Pulak, 'The Uluburun Shipwreck: An Overview' (1998); Eric Cline, '1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed' (2014).

nodes.label: The glazed moulded brick
nodes.full: To build a picture into a wall, Kassite craftsmen moulded bricks to interlocking shapes, coated them with an alkaline glaze coloured with copper for blue-green and lead-antimonate for yellow, fired them under controlled heat, and assembled them into a relief. The Uruk temple of Kara-indash is the earliest full example. It demanded mastery of moulding, of glaze chemistry, and of the kiln all at once.
nodes.src: Peter Moorey, 'Ancient Mesopotamian Materials and Industries' (1994); the Uruk facade in Ernst Heinrich (1982).

nodes.label: Glassmaking becomes a craft
nodes.full: Glassworkers learned to trail molten glass over a shaped core to make a small vessel, then pick out the core; to draw coloured canes and fuse them into mosaic patterns; and to cast inlays and beads. The fundamental recipe — silica fused with a soda flux and lime, coloured with metal oxides — was now understood well enough to be a guarded trade practice, written up in recipe form.
nodes.src: A. Leo Oppenheim et al., 'Glass and Glassmaking in Ancient Mesopotamia' (1970); Moorey (1994).

nodes.label: The war chariot at the centre of the army
nodes.full: The light, two-horse, spoked-wheel chariot carrying a driver and an archer was the striking arm of every Late Bronze army, Babylonia's included. It required a costly package — trained horses, a skilled crew, a workshop to build and repair it — so the chariot warrior became an elite, supported by a granted estate. Horse-training manuals circulated across the region to keep the teams battle-fit.
nodes.src: Robert Drews, 'The End of the Bronze Age' (1993); Mary Littauer & Joost Crouwel, 'Wheeled Vehicles and Ridden Animals in the Ancient Near East' (1979).

nodes.label: The first iron
nodes.full: A scatter of iron objects — a dagger, rings, a few tools — turns up in Kassite-era contexts, some worked from meteoric iron and a few possibly smelted. Iron at this date is rarer and dearer than gold, a diplomatic curiosity and a prestige metal. The knowledge to make it usable in quantity — carburising it to steel and quenching it — was still four centuries off.
nodes.src: Peter Moorey, 'Ancient Mesopotamian Materials and Industries' (1994); Jane Waldbaum, 'From Bronze to Iron' (1978).

nodes.label: Karduniash among the great powers
nodes.full: For most of this period Babylonia — Karduniash — was one of the small circle of Late Bronze Age great powers: Egypt, Hatti, Mitanni, Assyria, Elam and itself, whose kings dealt with one another on formal equal terms, forming alliances, arranging marriages, exchanging gifts, and complaining bitterly when they felt slighted. It is the only stretch of Babylonian history spent as an acknowledged equal in a system of comparable states.
nodes.src: Mario Liverani, 'Prestige and Interest' (1990); Trevor Bryce, 'Letters of the Great Kings of the Ancient Near East' (2003).

nodes.label: The Amarna letters of the Babylonian kings
nodes.full: Fourteen letters in the Egyptian archive at Amarna are to or from the Kassite court. In them Kadashman-Enlil I and Burna-Buriash II negotiate the marriage of a Babylonian princess to Pharaoh, argue over the amount and purity of the gold sent in return, complain that Babylonian envoys were kept waiting for years, and demand blood-price and restitution for a caravan of Babylonian merchants robbed and killed in Egyptian-held Canaan.
nodes.src: William Moran, 'The Amarna Letters' (1992), EA 1–14.

nodes.label: Lapis and horses for Egyptian gold
nodes.full: The staples of the Babylon–Egypt exchange were specific: Babylonian caravans carried lapis lazuli — bought from the east and re-sold at a markup — along with horses, chariots and worked luxuries, and brought back Egyptian gold, which Babylonian kings claimed was 'as plentiful as dust' in Pharaoh's land. Lapis made Babylonia the indispensable middleman between the mines of Afghanistan and the workshops of the Nile.
nodes.src: The Amarna gift-lists (Moran 1992); lapis routes in Daniel Potts, 'Mesopotamian Civilization' (1997).

nodes.label: Babylonia administers Dilmun
nodes.full: For part of the Kassite period Babylonia governed Dilmun — Bahrain — as a province. A Kassite governor resided at the walled city of Qal'at al-Bahrain, and his archive of Akkadian tablets — accounts, official letters, even a schoolboy's exercise — shows Babylonian administration and cuneiform literacy planted on the island. The old Gulf entrepôt was, for a while, under direct Mesopotamian rule.
nodes.src: The letters of the governor Ilī-ippašra; Steffen Terp Laursen & Piotr Steinkeller, 'Babylonia, the Gulf Region and the Indus' (2017).

nodes.label: The Suteans and the raided roads
nodes.full: The Sutean nomads of the Syrian steppe — and, from the twelfth century, the Aramaeans behind them — raided the Euphrates towns and preyed on the caravan roads throughout the period. It was a chronic, low-grade security problem that the peace of the Great Kings did nothing to solve, and it grew rapidly worse as the wider Bronze Age order began to break down.
nodes.src: J. A. Brinkman, 'Prelude to Empire: Babylonian Society and Politics, 747–626 B.C.' (1984), intro; the 'Sutû' in the Amarna and Kassite letters.

nodes.label: The end of the international system
nodes.full: Around 1200 the Late Bronze Age order came apart: the Hittite empire fell, the cities of the Levant and the Mycenaean world were destroyed, the 'Sea Peoples' moved, and the gift and tin routes dried up. Babylonia, further from the shock, weathered the first wave — but the collapse of its trading partners, together with the Assyrian occupation and the Elamite invasion, left the Kassite state hollow and ready to fall.
nodes.src: Eric Cline, '1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed' (2014); Robert Drews, 'The End of the Bronze Age' (1993).

nodes.label: Four centuries of stability
nodes.full: Set against the churn of the Old Babylonian kingdoms before and the Aramaean chaos to come, the Kassite centuries are an island of calm — one dynasty, one bounded country, one stable elite, one canonised culture. It is the period in which 'classical' Babylonia takes shape: the version of itself that later Assyrian, Persian and Greek observers treated as the ancient and authoritative model.
nodes.src: J. A. Brinkman, 'Materials and Studies for Kassite History' I (1976); the 'classical Babylonia' framing in Marc Van De Mieroop, 'A History of the Ancient Near East' (2016).

nodes.label: Karduniash — Babylonia becomes a country
nodes.full: Before the Kassites, 'Babylonia' was a shifting hegemony run from whichever city was on top. Under them it became a territorial state: a single name (Karduniash) used in the diplomatic correspondence, frontiers fixed by treaty with Assyria and Elam, one administration, and a shared identity that outlived the dynasty. The country that Nebuchadnezzar and Nabonidus later ruled was defined here.
nodes.src: Brinkman (1976); the frontier treaties in the 'Synchronistic History' and the Assyria–Babylonia boundary agreements.

nodes.label: The layered country
nodes.full: Kassite Babylonia was stratified by origin: the Kassite clans holding the crown, the army command and the great estates; the Akkadian-speaking Babylonian population in the towns and villages; Aramaean and Sutean newcomers thickening on the western fringe; and Elamites pressing from the east. That layering — a small foreign ruling caste over an old settled majority, with nomads on the edges — sets the pattern for the next five hundred years of Babylonian history.
nodes.src: Walter Sommerfeld, 'The Kassites of Ancient Mesopotamia' (CANE, 1995); Brinkman, 'Prelude to Empire' (1984).

nodes.label: The Bronze Age crisis and Babylonia's survival
nodes.full: The systemic crisis of around 1200 destroyed the Hittite empire, burned the cities of the Levant and Greece, and shook Egypt. Babylonia, further inland and fed from its own fields, rode out the first wave better than most. But weakened, cut off from its collapsed trading partners, and gutted by the Assyrian occupation, it fell to Elam in 1158 — and then, over the following century, to the Aramaean flood. The folio ends on the hinge into the early Iron Age dark centuries.
nodes.src: Eric Cline, '1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed' (2014); Brinkman, 'A Political History of Post-Kassite Babylonia' (1968).

nodes.label: The kudurru grantee
nodes.full: An official or an officer who had served the king well might receive an estate — its grant cut into a stone that stood in a temple, a clay copy kept on the land. He farmed it with tenants and dependents, owed the crown the service of a chariot and its crew, was often exempt from tax and corvée, and passed the whole arrangement to his son. He was a new kind of provincial power: land-rich, privileged, and only loosely tied to the throne.
nodes.src: Susanne Paulus, 'Die babylonischen Kudurru-Inschriften' (2014); Kathryn Slanski, 'The Babylonian Entitlement narûs' (2003).

nodes.label: The chariot warrior
nodes.full: The chariot fighter was the age's elite soldier the world over. He needed a trained team of horses, a workshop-built vehicle kept in repair, a composite bow and a driver, and an estate to pay for all of it. Across the Late Bronze kingdoms — Egypt, Hatti, Mitanni, Babylonia — this produced a hereditary warrior caste, and when the chariot armies were beaten around 1200 the states that rested on them fell with them.
nodes.src: Robert Drews, 'The End of the Bronze Age' (1993); the Babylonian chariotry in Brinkman (1976).

nodes.label: The scholar of the canonising age
nodes.full: The master scholar, the ummânu, collated manuscripts and fixed the standard editions, guarded knowledge marked 'secret' from the uninitiated, claimed descent from a founding scholar whose name he carried, trained apprentices in the closed disciplines, and stood at the king's side to read the omens before a war or an appointment. Learning had become a hereditary, prestigious and jealously bounded profession.
nodes.src: Alan Lenzi, 'Secrecy and the Gods' (2008); Paul-Alain Beaulieu on scribal ancestor-claims (2000).

nodes.label: The princess sent abroad
nodes.full: A Kassite king's daughter might be married to Pharaoh or to a Hittite king to seal an alliance — escorted west with a vast dowry and a retinue, never to return, her comfort and status a recurring worry in her father's letters, and her sons a possible future claim on a foreign throne. The diplomacy of the Great Kings was conducted between men and paid for, in exile, by their daughters.
nodes.src: The Amarna marriage negotiations (Moran, 'The Amarna Letters', 1992, EA 1–5); Samuel Meier, 'Diplomacy and International Marriages' (in Cohen & Westbrook, 2000).

nodes.label: The sufferer of Ludlul
nodes.full: The poem names him: Shubshi-meshre-Shakkan, a high official who — in its telling — fell from the king's favour, was struck with a wasting sickness no exorcist could name or cure, was robbed and abandoned by his own household, was mourned as already dead, and was then restored by Marduk in a series of dreams. It is one real man's account, however stylised, of total collapse and of what the silence of the gods feels like from inside.
nodes.src: W. G. Lambert, 'Babylonian Wisdom Literature' (1960); Amar Annus & Alan Lenzi, 'Ludlul bēl nēmeqi' (2010).
